stories.title: Inside LeBron's first game in Philly -- more than two decades ago
stories.summary: Nearly 25 years ago, LeBron won over Philly for the first time -- inside one of the most iconic basketball arenas in the world.
stories.detailText: THE FAX LAID out a grandiose plan. Jeremy Treatman, a former high school assistant coach in the Philadelphia suburbs who was running a burgeoning company that staged big-time basketball events between the game's future stars, had just sent a message to Dru Joyce II, the new coach at St. Vincent-St. Mary High School in Akron, Ohio, the school famously led by one of the most highly touted prep prospects in the history of the sport. It was the summer of 2002. Six months after a then-17-year-old LeBron James had appeared on the cover of Sports Illustrated accompanied by the headline, "The Chosen One," Treatman was pitching Joyce on choosing him to build James' hype even more. How would you like to play at the Palestra in Philly? How would you like to play Madison Square Garden against Sebastian Telfair? How would you like to play at Ohio State? How would you like to play at University of Dayton? How would you like to play in the Dean Dome in North Carolina? In Philly parlance, Treatman had him at, "Yo." "He calls me the next day and he says, 'You can get us to play at the Palestra?!'" Treatman told ESPN. "I go, 'Absolutely! Of course.' He goes, 'I've always dreamed of playing in the Palestra. I've heard about this place my whole life. "We're in.'" There was only one problem. "I was completely bluffing about the Palestra," Treatman said. "I hadn't talked to anybody." NAMED BY UNIVERSITY of Pennsylvania professor William N. Bates, evoking the Greek term "palæstra" that describes an athletic competition surrounded by an audience, the Palestra was the home for Penn's basketball, volleyball and wrestling teams. But its reputation as a hoops haven spread far beyond the corner of S. 33rd St. and Walnut St. on the Quakers' campus. With its red brick facade, its ceiling suspended by a spine of steel arches and bleachers that practically bleed right onto the maple hardwood playing surface, the Palestra became more than just a gymnasium, earning the nickname "The Cathedral of College Basketball." It was for decades the home for the famed round-robin Big Five schedule between Philadelphia's college basketball teams and has hosted more NCAA men's basketball games than any other arena in the country. "Brad Stevens and I, when I worked for him in Boston, we would go back and forth about Hinkle or the Palestra, Hinkle or the Palestra," Detroit Pistons assistant coach Jerome Allen told ESPN. Allen, a Penn alum, took umbrage with his old boss' preference for Butler University's bandbox. "[The Palestra] was built in 1926," Allen continued. "The first college game was played in '27. Cameron Indoor Stadium [at Duke University] was modeled after it. And everybody played in it: high school, college. It's a who's who for college basketball." (The NBA might have sided with Stevens by opting to have the NBA Cup final at Hinkle Fieldhouse this December. But Evan Wasch, the NBA's executive vice president of basketball strategy and growth, recently said the Palestra is "on the list" for consideration to host a future cup championship.) It was the perfect stage, Treatman thought, to host James, whom he first saw play in person at the Slam Dunk to the Beach tournament in Lewes, Delaware, in December 2001. "I saw him make an under-the-basket reverse layup that reminded me of Dr. J's move over Mark Landsberger," Treatman said, referring to Julius Erving's iconic bucket for the Philadelphia 76ers in Game 4 of the 1980 NBA Finals against the Los Angeles Lakers . Treatman pulled out his cellphone. With the image of a soaring James still fresh in his mind, he dialed Gregg Downer, the head coach at Lower Merion High School, where Treatman used to work as an assistant. "I called Downer and I said, 'I can't believe what I'm saying, but I think I just saw somebody who might be better than Kobe [Bryant],'" Treatman recalled. While Joyce prepared his team for James' senior season, Treatman began to make good on his bluff. He called Peggy Kowalski, the Palestra's box office manager, to get her on board, telling her he was "almost positive" the event would sell out. Now he just needed an opponent. He wanted to keep it local. "My idea was not to have them play the best team [in the country], but the best Philly team," Treatman said. He settled on Strawberry Mansion, a Philadelphia Public League school whose star, 6-foot-2 guard Maureece Rice, was threatening to break the high school scoring record of the man responsible for the most famous 100-point game in history: Wilt Chamberlain . The game was set: St. Vincent-St. Mary vs. Strawberry Mansion. James vs. Rice. Dec. 22, 2002, at the Palestra. "To have Bron there," Allen said, "everybody talked about the battle between him and Reece Rice." FIVE YEARS BEFORE Aron Cohen scored 14 points off the bench to help lift Penn over the Princeton Tigers as a junior guard, he was a high school sophomore sitting in the stands, soaking in the most raucous basketball environment he ever experienced -- before or since. "I just remember the Palestra being so packed," Cohen told ESPN. "I mean, when I played at Penn, we played against Carolina when they were No. 1 in the country. "And from what I remember, I felt like that game against LeBron was more packed. ... Just hearing about him, seeing him in SLAM magazine, it was like, 'Wow, this guy is in another world.' You have to see him. You can't miss it if you're a basketball fan." Former Detroit Pistons guard Richard Hamilton, whose Coatesville, Pennsylvania, high school team lost to Bryant and Lower Merion in the district playoffs at the Palestra in 1996, distinctly remembers the landmark game. "The Palestra is a big deal for us. That was always the mecca of Philadelphia for us," Hamilton told ESPN. "So when LeBron James comes there ... that was a moment for Philadelphia. Because it was before social media. Nobody got an opportunity to see him. So when you see this man-child coming to the arena with the type of aura that came with it, it was something that my friends and my family talk about to this day." Treatman delivered on his sellout prognostication -- and then some. "I had random people coming up to my office on the sixth floor at 1420 Walnut St., knocking on the door: 'You selling tickets? You selling tickets?'" Treatman said. "And I was. I was selling tickets. It was a one-man ticket office. It was hysterical. The phone calls were just nonstop. And the game, they tell me there were more people in the Palestra that night than any time in history." Among the attendees were current New York Knicks president of basketball operations Leon Rose, a then-influential sports agent who eventually signed James as a client. William Wesley, one of the sport's biggest power brokers, made an appearance. Cantankerous (and ubiquitous) Philadelphia sports radio personality Howard Eskin was there. A handful of Eagles players. Sixers star Allen Iverson -- just a year removed from winning MVP and taking Philadelphia all the way to the Finals against Bryant, Shaquille O'Neal and the Lakers -- was in the stands. But for James' team -- that had lost high-profile games the season before against other prominent foes in Oak Hill Academy (Virigina) and Amityville (New York) -- it was still a business trip. "I always speak about the abnormal becoming normal for us," said Romeo Travis, one of James' high school teammates who went on to become the University of Akron's all-time blocked shots leader before a long pro career overseas. "So we knew Iverson was coming, but it wasn't like, 'Oh my god, we got to play good for Iverson.' It was just like, 'OK.' It wasn't disrespectful or anything, because Iverson was still the man at that time, but it was just like, Shaq had just come to see us play." James' team was 6-0 to start the season, including a revenge 20-point victory over Oak Hill 10 days before, and was ranked No. 9 in the country, according to USA Today. They smashed Strawberry Mansion. SVSM went up 36-15 in the first half, using a full-court press that the home team couldn't handle. "The game was pretty much over pretty quickly," Cohen said. "St. Mary's was just way better. And LeBron had [an] early dunk and just set the whole place off, like, 'Ooh.'" Rice came into the game needing 80 points to break Chamberlain's Philadelphia high school scoring record of 2,252 points. He had zero at the break on 0-for-6 shooting. "The fans were on the floor talking crazy like, 'Yo, y'all stink! [Coming from] these cornfields [in Ohio]' and all that stuff," Travis remembered. "It was really cool, though. That was my favorite part about the experience, was the fans." Treatman, who now admits he "let in at least 150 extra people" beyond the 8,700-person Palestra capacity, started to get antsy. This wasn't what the proud Philly crowd came -- and paid -- to see. "It got really raunchy," Treatman said. "Gloria James got up and riled up the crowd. I thought there was going to be a riot. It was getting a little ugly in there." That's when LeBron James, nearly 25 years before signing with the Sixers and sending the city into another frenzy as a 41-year-old, won over Philly for the first time. THE SCORE HAD swelled to 65-25 in his team's favor after three quarters when James adjusted the game plan -- for both teams. When Rice hit a 3 early in the fourth quarter for just his second made basket of the night, James called for a clearout on Rice and pulled up to answer with a 3 of his own. Rice brought the ball up the floor and James stayed on him. Then Rice called for a clearout, too, feeling the juice of their back-and-forth. When Rice reached the wing, just above the 3-point line, he crossed his dribble left to right. James took a step backward, anticipating a drive, and both sneakers slipped underneath him. Rice crossed back through his legs, right to left, and with James scrambling to get back up from the floor, fired up another 3. He airballed the shot, but the mano-a-mano matchup was exactly what the fans had paid to see. Possession by possession, the Palestra's walls pulsated with their every move. "I've never heard a place louder than that ... ever," Cohen said. James came back down the court and answered with another 3. "This is when I realized LeBron James was a brilliant young man ... he noticed what was going on," Treatman said. "He felt the buzz, he felt the tension, and he called Maureece Rice over during live game action. He waved eight people away and they played one-on-one for four minutes. "They went up and down. Nobody else touched the ball for four minutes, and it was the most brilliant, incredible thing I've ever seen." Where Treatman saw showmanship, Travis saw a competitive zeal, the kind that has sustained his childhood friend through an NBA career in its 24th season. "How he became who he became is he didn't duck anybody," Travis said. "Anybody that said they were somebody, you had to show him proof. And Maureece Rice, even though they played different positions, they were saying he was one of the best in the country. OK, you're going to have to show and prove that. And you're going to have to come, and even if the game's over, you're going to have to show me something." James finished with 26 points, seven rebounds and seven assists. Rice, thanks to the late surge, ended up scoring 13. St. Vincent-St. Mary went on to win 85-47. "Growing up and being a historian and reading stories about the Palestra ... for us to go there my senior year, being from Akron, I was like, 'Oh, man, I'm in the building with some of the greatest that's ever played," James recalled on a recent episode of his podcast, "Mind the Game," with co-host Steve Nash. "It just had an aura about it, when I played there. It was fun." Nash asked James what stood out from his memories about the game all these years later: Iverson in the crowd and the name of his fourth-quarter rival in that packed gym in Philly, James said. "We were playing the No. 1 player in Pennsylvania, Maureece Rice," James added. "I'm reading all this stuff about Wilt and the history of the game, and we're traveling to Philadelphia. ... It was like, 'Oh shoot, we better have our shoes [tied] tight and we better be ready to go.'" Rice is 42 now, about six months older than James. He rarely posts anything about his basketball career on his Instagram account. But scroll down to 2021 and the second slide of a post showing an adolescent Rice cheesing for the camera while wearing a white No. 14 Charles Barkley USA Basketball jersey is a grainy clip of James talking about their showdown. "I respect Maureece a lot. He's one of the great players I've ever played against. I'm confident in him and I hope he keeps working. If he keeps working, he'll be a great player." Rice went on to play four years for George Washington University and spent a week on the Sixers' training camp roster in 2008 before continuing his career in the G League and abroad. James, in his first season in Philadelphia, has helped lead the Sixers to an 8-1 start, hoping to add to the four championships on his résumé before retiring. Cohen, who's fighting cancer, still plays pickup games at Penn on Saturday mornings. Watching James play basketball in Philadelphia gives him an escape just like it did when he was a high school kid. "I'm still in shock," Cohen said. "I'm like, 'LeBron James is a Sixer.' It's still surreal to me. ... I mean, for me personally, it's literally one of the most exciting, cool things to do in my life right now, is to just watch him and be a part of just the hoopla of knowing he's on our team." Travis spent time this summer golfing and hanging out with James and some of their high school teammates. He'll go see James and the Sixers play in person when Philadelphia rolls through Cleveland and Detroit this season -- easy car rides from his Ohio home. He would have seen him a lot more often had James signed with the Cavaliers, but he doesn't hold it against him. "I was confused, but I understood. He wanted to win," Travis said. "And I understand that, that he just wants to win and whatever it takes. I understand that completely and respect it. ... One of the great things about him is he does it his way." Treatman organized another showcase event featuring St. Vincent-St. Mary 17 years later in Columbus, Ohio, with James' alma mater facing Sierra Canyon High School, where James' son Bronny played. James squeezed in a visit to watch his son play in the game during a Lakers off day. It provided some full-circle nostalgia for Treatman, but even he says it wasn't the same as that December day in Philadelphia more than two decades ago. "It was something you've never seen before," he said. " [And] you've never seen again."

stories.title: Knicks 'appreciative' of Taylor Swift after Kolek, McBride question fandom
stories.summary: The Knicks have come to the defense of Taylor Swift and say they are "incredibly appreciative" of her support after Tyler Kolek and Miles "Deuce" McBride named her as the fakest celebrity fan at games.
stories.detailText: The Knicks have come to Taylor Swift's defense and said they are "incredibly appreciative" of her support after two New York players questioned whether she is a fake fan. During an NBA 2K League livestream posted on YouTube on Thursday, Tyler Kolek and Miles "Deuce" McBride were asked who was the fakest celebrity fan they had seen courtside at an NBA game. "At the Knicks games, I would say it's very performative because like they just want to be seen at the game. They're not necessarily fans. Probably Taylor Swift," Kolek answered and McBride agreed. Kolek acknowledged he was "going to get some hate from the Swifties" before adding "I guess she's got a lot going on, so she can't come all the time, but ... it's a little performative." McBride called other celebrity Knicks fans "solid," naming Ben Stiller and Tracy Morgan as examples. On Friday, a Knicks spokesperson responded to the players' comments in a statement. "Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization," the spokesperson said. Swift's wedding to Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce was held at Madison Square Garden in July. TMZ said her fandom of the Knicks stretches back to 2003, when she sang in a halftime talent contest at the age of 13. Swift was courtside for Game 4 of the NBA Finals in a "Stevie Knicks" T-Shirt, sitting next to friends Alana Haim, Este Haim and Mariska Hargitay. She also was courtside for Game 3 of the Eastern Conference finals when the Knicks played at the Cavaliers sitting with Kelce, who is a longtime Cleveland sports fan.

stories.title: Donovan Mitchell needs to shoot more, not less
stories.summary: The Cavs don’t need Donovan Mitchell to be someone he is not.
stories.detailText: OKLAHOMA CITY, OKLAHOMA - NOVEMBER 4: Donovan Mitchell #45 of the Cleveland Cavaliers walks down the floor during the second half against the Oklahoma City Thunder at Paycom Center on November 4, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. (Photo by Joshua Gateley/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you’ve been online recently, you may have noticed that Donovan Mitchell has… pissed off a lot of Cleveland Cavaliers fans. Twitter is ablaze with criticism. People want him traded. Some regret that he was ever traded for . Mitchell has become the crux of all problems; the shot-chucking ‘dictator’ who will never be the primary option on a championship team. But everyone has it backwards; Donovan Mitchell needs to shoot more . Mitchell’s field goal attempts and usage rate are at career lows to start the year. His assist percentage and shot chart are nearly identical to previous seasons. That means Mitchell has less control over the offense than ever, despite some insisting that he’s grown into a ball-dominant tyrant. How did we get here? And why are fans feeling such a disconnect? Mitchell has always been a scorer more than a passer. He currently ranks in the 41st percentile in assist-to-usage ratio — a stat that tracks how often a player is ending their possessions with an assist rather than a shot attempt or turnover. This means that roughly half of the league’s players are more likely to get an assist on any given possession than Donovan Mitchell. That can lead to games where it feels like Mitchell is hogging the ball while leaving his teammates hanging. That gung-ho play style caused some frustration throughout last year’s playoffs, and the complaints have carried into this year. Fans want to know why Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen aren’t getting the ball. Why do their leads disappear so often? And why haven’t the Cavs gotten over the hump despite a roaring regular season? Some have identified Mitchell’s lack of playmaking as the problem. Which, in fairness, is certainly a factor. Cleveland has lost big games in the past due to Mitchell’s shot selection. He doesn’t always make the right decision with the ball in his hands — and that can be difficult to watch as a fan. But we should reframe this discussion. Let’s start here. Donovan Mitchell isn’t a point guard. And maybe, he doesn’t have to be. Shai-Gilgeous Alexander was in the 29th percentile for assist-to-usage ratio when the Oklahoma City Thunder won the championship. He’s in the 0th percentile now. Some people score; others pass. The truth is, championship-caliber players are allowed to have weak points. You are not disqualified if you can’t do everything on your own. Giannis Antetokounmpo never learned how to shoot. Nikola Jokic never became an elite defender. And the New York Knicks didn’t win a championship last June because Jalen Brunson suddenly became an elite playmaker — they won because they delegated more playmaking responsibilities to Karl-Anthony Towns — leaving space for Brunson to do what Brunson does best… score the ball. All of those teams identified their star’s weakness, and built a roster around them that could insulate them. The Cavs need a similar solution. They need someone who can take playmaking off of Mitchell’s plate. Darius Garland was the original fit. And, for a while, he would thread the needle beautifully. He sent the defense scattering into motion while Mitchell would catch the ball against a defense already on their back feet. That dynamic led to 64 wins — but unfortunately, Garland couldn’t stay healthy. James Harden was the next option. He’s been more available than Garland, which was enough to help bolster the team to an Eastern Conference Finals run. But Harden’s style differs from Garland’s. He’s slower-paced, favoring a heliocentric style that inhibits stationary spacing around him. The result is fewer chances for Mitchell to attack in motion, nerfing his greatest strength as a slasher who can attack gaps. All of this has culminated in the Cavs (and fans online) asking Mitchell to be more of a playmaker. But that is a fundamental misunderstanding of who he is — and how you win in the NBA by playing to your strengths. Let’s back up for a second. I want to be clear that I am not advocating for Mitchell to go full Dion Waiters and ignore the other four Cavaliers sharing the court with him at any given time. He still needs to pass the ball — and he needs to choose the right moments to assert himself as a scorer. You can’t win by playing like a bull in a China shop. There has to be a delicate balance between scoring in bunches and releasing control of the offense to someone else. That’s the key here. Mitchell will never be a point guard. Any system that asks him to make reads at that level will learn the hard way. You can’t force a square peg into a round hole. You can, however, build a competitive team that understands who Mitchell is. We know for a fact that Mitchell can go nuclear as a scorer in the playoffs. We’ve seen it multiple times. But who can grab the reins and facilitate those high-scoring performances? Who is the Karl-Anthony Towns to his Jalen Brunson in this scenario? The Cavs are still hoping that will be Harden. Additional support from Mobley would be welcomed. Whether that will be enough is certainly worth questioning. But here’s another cold, hard truth: Making it to the top of the mountain is hard. If we’re being honest, it’s damn near impossible. This franchise had the greatest player alive for 11 seasons and only made it to the finish line once. Cleveland would need a myriad of miracles to win a championship with this group. Even if everything went right, they could still fall short. That’s just the way it goes. That’s why sticking true to your identity is more important than anything. Being a bad version of someone else will always be inferior to being the best version of yourself. I don’t think Mitchell will lead Cleveland to a title through his playmaking. That feels like jumping the shark. The Cavs do need him to be better defensively and to make better reads offensively, but that doesn’t necessarily mean relinquishing his role as one of the highest-volume scorers in the league. That’s who he is — that’s who the team traded for. Mitchell needs to be a world-class scorer. Nearly all of his attention on offense should be centered on getting his shot. Passing will always come second. Winning or losing comes down to Mitchell taking and making the big shots. That was the primary difference between him and Brunson last season. Of course, any team would prefer a superstar who is capable of blending elite scoring with masterful playmaking and impactful defense. But, you work with what you have — and the Cavs have a dynamic scorer, not a floor general. Accepting Mitchell’s true nature and having the supporting cast insulate him with their playmaking is the most realistic path forward. It’s the only path forward.

stories.title: Knicks defend Taylor Swift's fandom after Tyler Kolek, Miles McBride weigh in
stories.summary: Swift's history at Madison Square Garden includes courtside appearances dating back to 2014 and her July wedding to Travis Kelce.
stories.detailText: Taylor Swift's New York Knicks fandom is up for debate -- and the team itself has already weighed in. In an NBA 2K League video shared Thursday, Knicks guards Tyler Kolek and Miles McBride were asked to name the "fakest" celebrity fan they'd seen courtside at an NBA game. Kolek floated Swift's name, and McBride agreed. "Maybe Taylor Swift? I don't know if I've seen her at any other games," Kolek said of the pop star's appearance at Game 4 of the NBA Finals . Kolek acknowledged that Swift's schedule might keep her from getting to Madison Square Garden regularly, but he still referred to her fandom as "a little performative." McBride pointed to two familiar faces at the Garden -- Ben Stiller and Tracy Morgan -- as examples of "solid" celebrity fans. The Knicks, meanwhile, had a different read on Swift's courtside credentials. "Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization," the team said in a statement to TMZ . Swift has been photographed at Knicks games as far back as 2014, seven years before McBride joined the team and a decade before Kolek did. She was last seen courtside at MSG on June 10, when the Knicks completed the largest comeback in NBA Finals history , overcoming a 29-point deficit in a 107-106 victory over the San Antonio Spurs . Less than a month later, she r eturned to the Garden for her star-studded wedding to Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce on July 3. As for how Swift's fans might take the clip, Kolek had an idea. "I'm going to get some hate from the Swifties," he said.

stories.title: Westchester Knicks 2026-27 Season Primer
stories.summary: Three two-way players, a returning prospect, and a collection of NBA hopefuls open their season tonight in Maine.
stories.detailText: WHITE PLAINS, NY - FEBRUARY 21: Dink Pate #1 of the Westchester Knicks drives to the basket during the game against the Cleveland Charge on February 21, 2026 at Westchester County Center in White Plains, NY. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Luther Schlaifer/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images New York’s G League affiliate opens its 2026-27 season tonight against the Maine Celtics in the Tip-Off Tournament. The roster features three players on two-way contracts, a returning fan favorite (hint: he’s great on toast), and a collection of prospects hoping to dribble their way up to an NBA court. With the Knicks operating near the second apron, Westchester provides a way to develop young players without committing additional standard roster spots. Two-way players can spend most of the season in White Plains while remaining available for NBA duty, subject to a limit of up to 50 games on the active roster. The G League has also given players like Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek opportunities to get more work. Here’s a peek at the players worth watching. Dalton Knecht: A second chance in New York Of everyone on Westchester’s roster, Dalton Knecht has the clearest path to helping the big club this season. The 2024 first-round pick (17th overall) arrived after the Lakers waived him, with New York releasing Kevin McCullar Jr. to make room for Knecht on a two-way contract. This low-risk move could pay off if the former Tennessee star rediscovers his shooting touch and improves his court awareness, which was a criticism raised in the comments section at Silver Screen and Roll . The 25-year-old made a promising debut for the New York Knicks this week, scoring 10 points on efficient 4-of-6 shooting (including two threes) with seven boards, a dime, and a block in 16 minutes off the bench in a rout of the Bulls. Finding consistent playing time will be difficult, however. With Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, Pacôme Dadiet, and Mohamed Diawara competing for minutes on the wings, Knecht will probably need an injury or another opening to receive an extended look. (TBH, he already looks ahead of Dadiet.) Coach Mike Brown has said he’d rather see Knecht playing meaningful minutes in the G League than sitting on the NBA bench. Makes sense. Knecht needs opportunities to shoot, make decisions, and work through mistakes. He has shown he can score, but questions remain about his defense, shot selection, and ability to contribute consistently as a role player. If Knecht performs well enough, the organization could eventually consider converting him to a standard NBA contract, which would require sufficient roster and financial room. For now, he should get plenty of opportunities to let it fly against G League competition. Tyler Nickel: A sniper Speaking of flamethrowers . . . Tyler “Silent K” Nickel might be the most straightforward fit for what the Knicks need. New York selected the Vanderbilt sharpshooter with the 47th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft after an impressive senior season. He followed that with a promising Summer League showing and signed a two-way contract. From what we’ve seen, Nickel moves well without the ball, finds open space, and punishes defenses for leaving him unattended. The big league Knicks have several players capable of creating offense, and a dependable perimeter shooter who doesn’t require many touches could fit nicely alongside them (see: Landry Shamet). His defense will help determine how quickly the 23-year-old advances. He needs to prove he can handle quicker, stronger NBA bodies while maintaining his shooting efficiency against more aggressive closeouts. Westchester should give him plenty of reps to work on both. Nickel doesn’t seem to have Knecht’s offensive versatility, but his shooting gives him a clearly defined role. If he can hold his own defensively, he could become a useful option for additional spacing. For the time being, Westchester might have its very own set of Splash Brothers to keep you entertained (at a reasonable price). Jaden Akins: Defense and versatility Jaden Akins took a less direct route to New York. Undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025, he spent last season with the Motor City Cruise after earning All-Big Ten third-team and All-Defensive recognition as a senior. His combination of scoring, secondary playmaking, and defense caught the Knicks’ attention. Westchester acquired his returning player rights in September, and he secured a two-way contract before the season. Akins faces considerable competition at the one- and two-guard spots. His best chance of separating himself is to use his time at Westchester to polish his defense and his work off the ball. Can he defend multiple positions, run an offense for stretches, and make open shots? Can he contribute consistently without committing unnecessary fouls or turnovers? Those qualities will probably matter more to New York than his individual scoring averages. Dink Pate: Back for another season The fan favorite returns! Dink Pate returns to Westchester after a confusing offseason. The 6’8” wing, still only 20 years old, averaged approximately 16 points, seven rebounds, and four assists across 50 games with the club last season. He subsequently attempted to play college basketball at Providence, but that plan fell through amid questions about his NCAA eligibility. The Knicks signed and waived him on an Exhibit 10 contract, and he returned to Westchester, which already held his G League rights. Pate has length, can create his own offense, and contributes as a rebounder and passer. His combination of physical tools and professional experience makes him one of Westchester’s more interesting developmental players. Decision-making and efficiency are where he needs improvement. Unlike Knecht, Nickel, and Akins, Pate doesn’t have a two-way contract. He would need an available two-way or standard roster spot and a new NBA contract to join the big club. Westchester’s rights also don’t prevent another NBA team from signing him. Thus, his time in White Plains is a prove-it run for a broader audience—so we expect to see some inspired hooping from him this season. Frontcourt depth: Robbins, Dante, and Miličić Westchester’s frontcourt includes several players who could provide useful depth. Liam Robbins , a seven-footer who went undrafted out of Vanderbilt in 2023, is probably the most recognizable. He showed some encouraging work around the iron during Summer League with the Knicks, and Westchester subsequently acquired his G League rights. Robbins brings size, rebounding, and shot-blocking ability. The big league club could use more reliable center depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond, with James Wiseman slow to make an impression. Robbins could use his time in White Plains to convince the team he deserves a look—perhaps before the front office starts eyeing its surplus of guards as trade bait. N’Faly Dante , the 6-foot-11 former Oregon center, is working his way back from an ACL injury. His size and athleticism lift our eyebrows, but getting healthy and regaining his previous form will be the immediate priorities. Igor Miličić Jr. , a 6-foot-10 forward out of Tennessee, brings international experience and positional versatility after spending time with the Delaware Blue Coats last season. Improving his outside shooting and defensive consistency would help him take the next step. The wings: Jourdain, Okani, and company Westchester also has several forwards competing for rotation minutes. Nick Jourdain returns after averaging roughly eight points and more than five rebounds last season. The former Memphis forward provides rebounding, energy, and defensive effort. His journey from local tryout to returning player is a nice story, even if an NBA opportunity remains a longer shot. Toby Okani , the former West Virginia wing, brings length and athleticism after spending time with multiple G League organizations. David Dixon , an undrafted forward out of Duquesne, and Tahj-Malik Campbell are also trying to establish roles after joining the training camp group. The guards: Shooting potential Westchester’s backcourt includes several capable players. Mitchell Mascari is worth watching after arriving from the Stockton Kings. The 6’5” guard shot approximately 42% from downtown last season, giving Westchester another option to stretch the floor. Paul Zilinskas returns as a scoring option at guard and on the wing, while Amir “Primo” Spears joins the club after being selected 25th in the 2026 G League Draft. Spears brings extensive college experience, including a productive stint at UTSA, and spent last season playing professionally in Mexico. The road begins in Maine The three two-way players will receive the most attention this season, although we’ll also keep an eye on Pate (‘cuz he’s kinda electric). The rest of the roster will compete for minutes and try to establish themselves as dependable professional players. Westchester opens its Tip-Off Tournament schedule tonight at 7 p.m. against the Maine Celtics at the Portland Expo, then faces the same opponent at the same venue Sunday at 12:30 p.m. Both games will air on MSG Network. Go W-Knicks!

stories.title: Report: Warriors contact Bulls, Pelicans, and Bucks about Kristaps Porzingis trade
stories.summary: The Golden State Warriors have called the Pelicans, Chicago Bulls, and Milwaukee Bucks about a Kristaps Porzingis trade.
stories.detailText: SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA - MARCH 10: Jalen Smith #25 of the Chicago Bulls goes up for a shot on Kristaps Porzingis #7 of the Golden State Warriors during the first half at Chase Center on March 10, 2026 in San Francisco, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Golden State Warriors have contacted the New Orleans Pelicans, Chicago Bulls, and Milwaukee Bucks to gauge the organization’s interest in a potential trade for center Kristaps Porzingis (or really his contract), per a report by Brett Siegel of ClutchPoints. With Porzingis likely headed for retirement and accepting the Warriors withholding his salary, Siegel reports that he is expected to accept a significant buyout from his $20 million salary. The Dubs front office is trying to use his contract as a trade exception in the next month to solidify the team’s depth without limiting their options at the trade deadline. “Among the many teams the Warriors have contacted since the start of the season, as reported earlier on Friday in our weekly newsletter , ClutchPoints has been able to confirm with league sources three teams in particular: the Milwaukee Bucks, Chicago Bulls, and New Orleans Pelicans,” Siegel wrote. The Warriors interest in Pelicans wings Trey Murphy III and Herb Jones has been reported on for years, and the Dubs reportedly called New Orleans about center Yves Missi earlier this season as well. However, the fact that the two sides have not previously agreed to a deal should leave fans skeptical that a deal will happen now (especially months before the trade deadline). Siegel’s reporting suggests the Warriors and Bucks were not close to a deal for Myles Turner, with different evaluations of his contract’s value. As for the Bulls, Siegel highlighted center Jalen Smith. “Going back to the topic of potential trade suitors for Porzingis, the Warriors showed interest in Bulls’ center Jalen Smith in a potential Porzingis-oriented deal with Chicago, but the Bulls have not shown a willingness to make such a move at this time, sources said,” Siegel said. “The Bulls are wanting to evaluate their roster and potential moves closer to the trade deadline unless draft compensation is included, despite opening the year as one of the worst teams in the NBA.” Smith would be an excellent to the Warriors current front court depth. While he lacks the explosive ceiling that Golden State hoped to get from Porzingis, he is an incredibly well rounded role player who would give head coach Steve Kerr another center who can shoot threes other than 40-year old Al Horford. The 10th overall pick in the 2020 NBA Draft by the Phoenix Suns, Smith never found his footing in Phoenix and was quickly viewed around the league as a bust before finding consistency with the Indiana Pacers. Over the past five seasons, split between Indiana and Chicago, Smith has averaged 9.4 points, 5.9 rebounds, and 0.8 blocks on 50.1%/34.3%/74.9% shooting in 18.0 minutes per game (254 games, 76 starts). Still only 26, Smith has been the primary starting center for the first time in his career this season. While he is posting career highs in minutes (22.5), points (11.0), rebounds (7.8), assists (1.8), and blocks (0.9) per game so far this season, the Bulls are 1-7 and have been among the worst teams in the league. Slated to be a free agent at the end of the season, Smith seems destined to be traded before the deadline for a package built around second-round picks. The question is, will the Warriors be able to convince the Bulls to make that move before the new year? The Warriors only have two tradeable second round picks, one in 2030 and another in 2033. One added enticement they could add to a deal with the Bulls, who have notoriously cheap owner Jerry Reinsdorf, would be to take back either Buddy Hield or Zach Collins alongside Smith. The Warriors would likely waive either player, but would effectively be taking $18-$19 million off the Bulls books. Assuming the Bulls agreed to a buyout with Porzingis in the $6-8 million range that Siegel speculates, Bulls ownership could save around $10 million.

stories.title: The best version of Devin Booker is the one attacking early
stories.summary: Historical numbers suggest that an aggressive first-half Booker gives Phoenix a significantly better chance to win. Because duh.
stories.detailText: PHOENIX, AZ - NOVEMBER 5: Devin Booker #15 of the Phoenix Suns shoots the ball during the game against the Orlando Magic on November 5, 2026 at Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix, Arizona. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Barry Gossage/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Sometimes all it takes is a spark, however small, to start a fire and change a team’s trajectory. Even if that spark comes against an opponent you wouldn’t necessarily consider quality. The Phoenix Suns’ 117-104 victory over the Orlando Magic might be that spark, although with Houston and San Antonio staring them down on the schedule over the next few days, there’s a chance we won’t look back at this game as the moment that ignited some great blaze. But there were things we witnessed that can be deposited into the old adjustments bank, lessons that could serve as valuable reference points when trying to manufacture future victories. One of those lessons, as obvious as it might seem, is that feeding Devin Booker early remains one of the best ways to give this team an opportunity to win basketball games. Booker is the $57 million man, and constructing a roster that forces him to assume duplicative responsibilities within the starting lineup isn’t exactly ideal. Too often, we see Booker drift away from his natural role as a shooting guard and become the primary playmaker, tasked with creating opportunities for everyone else rather than focusing on what he does best. Against Orlando, we saw something different. In the first half, Booker went 8-of-13 from the field, including 3-of-4 from beyond the arc and a perfect 4-of-4 from the free-throw line, scoring 23 points while establishing himself as the focal point of the offense. Granted, this was the Orlando Magic. Quality opponents have demonstrated the ability to scheme Booker out of games, as we saw earlier this season against a shorthanded Oklahoma City Thunder team. And that’s precisely why the argument for having a quality facilitator persists. When you have somebody capable of assuming the responsibility of distributing the basketball, opposing defenses have another variable to account for. They have to dedicate attention to disrupting that player’s ability to initiate the offense, which can create more opportunities for Booker to operate as a scorer. And when Booker gets going early, it creates opportunities for everyone around him. As he begins to command the defensive gravity we know he possesses, teammates find themselves with more space and cleaner looks. The hope is that by the time an opposing defense figures out how to slow him down, Booker has already inflicted enough damage to force them into scrambling, opening up opportunities for the rest of the roster to capitalize. Getting Devin Booker engaged early should be the North Star for this team. If opposing defenses are finding ways to take the ball out of his hands, then it’s the coaching staff’s responsibility to scheme ways to get it back into his hands in situations where he can be effective. Here’s a fun stat for you. Throughout his career, Booker has attempted 13 or more field goals in the first half of a game 110 times. In those games, the Suns have a .582 winning percentage. And when Booker does what he did last night, shooting 60% or better from the field while attempting at least 13 shots in the first half, that winning percentage climbs to .727. What’s interesting is that since the acquisition of Bradley Beal prior to the 2023-24 season, Booker has attempted 13 or more field goals in the first half 30 times. The other 80 times occurred pre-Beal, with 46 occurring alongside Chris Paul. Devin Booker went 8-of-13 in the first half against Orlando. Fun stat: When Booker attempts 13+ shots in the first half, the Suns are 64–46 (.582) in his career. When he shoots 60% or better on 13+ first-half attempts? That winning percentage jumps to .727. Feed Book early. pic.twitter.com/T4Hz0F22e0 — John Voita, III (@DarthVoita) November 6, 2026 I’m certainly not breaking any new ground by suggesting that your most skilled scorer should be looking to score early and often, especially when doing so creates opportunities for the players around him. But that’s exactly what we witnessed against Orlando. Booker scored only seven points in the second half, yet he added four assists as Dillon Brooks and Miles Bridges began finding more opportunities to contribute offensively, benefiting from the defensive gravity Booker had established earlier in the game. Perhaps this needs to become a point of emphasis for the coaching staff, along with a mental adjustment for Booker himself. Because when you look at the rosters he’s played alongside since Chris Paul left town, it’s difficult to argue that they’ve consistently been constructed to maximize his greatest strength, which can create a malaise and affinity for falling into distribution responsibilities rather than getting yours. Playing alongside Bradley Beal, whose availability was frequently compromised by injuries, eventually led to stretches in which Eric Gordon or Tyus Jones ran the offense. Now Booker finds himself sharing the backcourt with Jalen Green, another player whose natural instincts lean toward scoring rather than facilitating. None of those combinations has been particularly conducive to allowing Booker to operate consistently in the role where he’s most dangerous. While there are legitimate criticisms of Booker’s game, particularly his struggles executing in clutch situations and the difficulties he encounters when more physical defenders impose their will on him, those concerns shouldn’t prevent us from recognizing what he does well. When Booker establishes himself offensively early, forces defenses to react, and creates opportunities for his teammates to capitalize, that’s the version of Devin Booker this team needs. And when that approach contributes to a much-needed victory, it deserves recognition and applause. The Suns aren’t going to solve every roster deficiency overnight, and the challenges of getting Booker quality looks against better competition aren’t going anywhere. But there’s something to be said for simplifying the approach and putting your best player in positions to succeed. Orlando provided a reminder of what happens when Booker dictates the offense rather than reacting to it. If Phoenix is searching for a spark that can become something sustainable, getting Booker going early seems like a pretty damn good place to start.

stories.title: Walker Kessler is having more of an impact than it looks
stories.summary: On Walker Kessler’s quiet dominance, and how he’s proven critical to the Lakers’ early season success.
stories.detailText: Since the Lakers acquired Walker Kessler over the summer, most of the conversation regarding his play, and subsequent impact, has been tied to the cost paid to land him. The multiple years and millions of dollars, the draft picks and swaps, each have served as footnotes after every game thus far. While fair given what the Lakers need from him going forward, it has also put increased emphasis on his raw production rather than influence. If you’re into that kind of thing, Kessler’s per-game numbers are solid. His 14.4 points, 10.2 rebounds and four stocks nightly will play. However, it doesn’t capture the full spectrum of his impact. On offense, Kessler is still navigating life as Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves’ screener. It’s an entirely new world compared to the barren guard groups he played next to with the Utah Jazz. Things like timing, pick angles and court-mapping will take time. But the early results have been encouraging nevertheless. After his dunk-centric eruption on opening night, defenses have already begun selling out in the paint to take away his lob and cut chances. Due to this, Kessler has not been able to duplicate his scoring outbursts, but it hasn’t lessened his value to the offense either. A direct result of teams loading up and tagging Kessler — often with multiple defenders — is that it has created open shots from the perimeter, as seen in the clips below. Walker Kessler scored just 2 points, but his roll gravity drew Utah’s defense and created wide-open threes. The Lakers went 20/47 (43%) from deep. pic.twitter.com/y7X8Ui6GAG — Lakers24Eight (@lakers24ate) October 26, 2026 Kessler’s roll gravity also extends to his rebounding ability. As one of the league’s best second-chance creators, and simply being a massive person, Kessler often draws multiple players to him whenever a shot goes up. This fear is well warranted. The Lakers’ offensive rebound percentage jolts up nearly 10% when Kessler is on the floor compared to off. Like a black hole, this sucks up defenders from the corners and creates quality looks for shooters. The Lakers are currently shooting 43.9% from the corners this season, the second-best mark in the league. Beyond the attention Kessler attracts on offense simply from existing, his omnipresence is probably best demonstrated with the impact he’s had on the Lakers’ defense. As the backbone and backline, Kessler’s presence in the paint has allowed the team’s wings to be extremely aggressive shocking the ball with the trust that the center will clean up any mistakes. This disruptive style has resulted in the Lakers being one of the best defenses in terms of forced turnovers. And when his teammates do get burned for gambling or getting blown by, Kessler has been iron-clad protecting the basket. Not only are opposing teams shooting just 26.9% of their shots at the rim when Kessler is on the floor — would rank fourth-best in the NBA — they are also missing once he meets them there. Among the 12 players who have defended at least 50 shots within six feet this season, Kessler ranks first in defended shooting percentage against (45.1%) while also contesting the second-most attempts behind only Victor Wembanyama, according to the league’s tracking data . Last night Walker Kessler contested 14 Warriors shots, they made 3 of them. Some, were missed threes, but a lot were contests in the paint including five blocks. pic.twitter.com/9RThoBA0DI — Iztok Franko (@iztok_franko) October 31, 2026 Kessler’s deterrence and effectiveness in shutting off the paint is not solely due to his size. His height and frightening wingspan do help, yes. But what drives his success is his impressive motor. With every second jump contest, race down the floor and closeout to a 3-point shooter, Kessler’s care factor is never in doubt. That goes a long way to actualizing his defensive upside. Despite how hard he ultimately tries, the Lakers are learning firsthand that Kessler can’t be everywhere at once. This is never more true than the defensive drop-off once he’s on the bench. Through their first nine games, the Lakers have allowed a defensive rating of 110.1 with Kessler on the court compared to 117.2 when he’s been off. That’s a discrepancy that is the equivalent of the team performing like the eighth-best defense versus the 26th. While his individual numbers will likely fluctuate nightly, and even quarterly, as illustrated by his dominant final frame — 10 points, five rebounds, four blocks and a steal — against the Sacramento Kings on Wednesday, Kessler has proven to be more than suited for the role bestowed upon him. He may not be the thundering force that Dončić is or as crafty as Reaves, but Kessler’s job as the Lakers’ silent protector has been as critical to the team’s strong start. It won’t always look like he’s had a good game in the box score. But just watch how that opposing ball-handler goes wide-eyed and makes a U-turn when the giant in purple and gold makes his stand. More than any numbers can ever quantify, Kessler’s game is measured in fear. And the Lakers are benefiting from it so far. All stats courtesy of Cleaning the Glass unless otherwise stated. Kolek didn't hesitate to name a major celebrity. Kolek promptly named pop superstar Taylor Swift , who made headlines for her courtside appearance at Game 4 of the Knicks’ series against the San Antonio Spurs on June 10, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. stories.title: Report: Warriors expected to trade Kristaps Porzingis by December 16th
stories.summary: The Golden State Warriors are expected to trade Kristaps Porzingis prior to December 16th, per Brett Siegel.
stories.detailText: SACRAMENTO, CA - APRIL 10: Kristaps Porzingis #7 of the Golden State Warriors looks on during the game against the Sacramento Kings on April 10, 2026 at Golden 1 Center in Sacramento, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Rocky Widner/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The Golden State Warriors Kristaps Porzingis saga is expected to come to an end before the end of the year, according to a report by Brett Siegel of ClutchPoints . Porzingis, who re-signed with the Dubs last season on a partially guaranteed two-year, $40 million deal, opted not to join the team for training camp and has accepted not receiving payments , seemingly deciding to retire. However, hoping to make the best out of an unexpected situation, the Warriors are hoping to use Porzingis’ salary essentially as a trade exception. While that was all known, Siegel’s reporting suggests the front office is expected to trade Porzingis by December 16th. “For starters, Porzingis’ time with the Warriors is over,” Siegel wrote. “He will not be playing another game for this franchise, as ClutchPoints reported on Oct. 23 before the team’s first game of the season, and it’s almost a given he will be traded, likely within the next 30-40 days… Much like how the Warriors traded for Dennis Schroder in the middle of December during the 2024-25 season, only to re-aggregate him in a bigger deal for Jimmy Butler at the trade deadline, league sources are anticipating a similar strategy this time around with Porzingis.” Siegel notes that players who signed free agent contracts this offseason will all become trade-eligible on December 15th, which will also give teams more options on that day. Moreover, December 16th is the deadline for a player to be traded and still be eligible to be aggregated in a deal at the trade deadline in February. So while it’s definitely possible for a deal to be made sooner, that effectively becomes the deadline for the Warriors front office if they would like to make a smaller move with Porzingis that would leave them flexibility to still go looking for bigger fish at the deadline. Siegel’s reporting does not even engage with a scenario where the Warriors do not trade Porzingis in December. It’s worth wondering if they would simply hold onto him until the trade deadline if they did not receive an offer that enticed them enough before. With the Warriors 6-3 and looking like a legit playoff team, though, the front office should be less inclined to slow play adding depth to the roster.

stories.title: Windhorst & MacMahon: What league insiders are seeing from Philly's 8-1 start
stories.summary: Brian Windhorst and Tim MacMahon canvass the league for early superteam intel, the staying power of Memphis and next steps in Sacramento.
stories.detailText: Early in the NBA season, bad surprises receive more attention than the good ones. For teams in the occasional negative spotlight, it's annoying and they often complain about it and quite fairly. But it's the nature of a high-profile, high-stakes business. And there will be plenty of that in this weekly space, but this week there's a pull toward some of the more pleasant developments with the 2026-27 season in its third week. The advance scouts and pro personnel directors have made their first loops and filed their initial reports. Assistant coaches have seen the first rounds of film as they prepare for opponents. We've talked to them and others and here's some of what they're saying about two of the hottest teams in the league, plus the next steps for What is the league making of the Philadelphia 76ers ' start? Brian Windhorst: The term superteam is often overused, but with five Most Valuable Player awards and five Finals MVP awards on this roster, it qualifies. Historically, superteams see their offense lag behind their defense early as stars settle into their roles. This was true of the 2007-08 Boston Celtics , who averaged just 93.5 points over their first 10 games but were No. 1 on defense from day one. In 2010-11, the Miami Heat had a top-five defense right away but sluggish offensive nights contributed to a 9-8 start. Add the 2026-27 Sixers to the list, with Philly languishing in the bottom 10 in offensive efficiency but boasting a top-three defense. That stinginess is a major reason for the 76ers' 4-0 road record, including wins against the New York Knicks on opening night and Detroit Pistons on Wednesday . And LeBron James , Jaylen Brown , Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey are owning clutch time. "They've been terrific in the clutch and I haven't seen much clunkiness or indecisiveness in them at all in the games I've watched," an Eastern Conference scout told ESPN. "They also aren't turning the ball over, which you expect to see with a bunch of new guys playing together." The 76ers are 7-0 this season in games that have entered clutch time -- defined as the score being within five points in the final five minutes -- the driving force of their league-best 8-1 record. It's not prudent to jump to conclusions or to overanalyze it, but it's fair to say it has been a very good sign. And league personnel have a reason. "It's Maxey," an East executive said. "He's making them go and you can see he already has all of their trust in fourth quarters. LeBron definitely trusts him and they've already really developed a nice two-man game that stresses defenses." Another East executive said, "LeBron brings a lot of things when he comes to your team. And we've seen it before, he raises everyone's level. Maxey was already a great player, but he's also raised his level and some of that has to be having LeBron there." Tim MacMahon: There were a lot of questions -- and doubts -- around the league about how the Sixers' four All-Stars would mesh. As much as egos were considered a potential obstacle, it has been interesting to see Maxey, the least decorated of the quartet, emerge as the clear No. 1 option. He has been the primary reason that Philadelphia keeps pulling out close wins, ranking third in the league with 21 points in 19 clutch minutes. "He comes and gets the first bucket or two of the fourth and ... 'Here it comes, here it comes,'" 76ers coach Nick Nurse said of the 26-year-old guard. "In an incredibly humble way, he just seems like he knows he's really good. I don't know if I've sensed that until this year." Windhorst: Another factor league insiders have noticed is the working relationship James already has built with his new coach. They didn't have a previous relationship, but James and Nurse had an extensive conversation before James chose the 76ers in free agency. They talked several times before the start of training camp, establishing an important base. That might seem like something that would be taken for granted. Considering James' history when joining a new team, it shouldn't. "LeBron didn't vibe with [Heat coach Erik Spoelstra] at the start, and lots of people think he wanted him fired in the first month [of 2010-11]," one veteran NBA executive said. "He never gave David Blatt a chance (when James went back to the Cleveland Cavaliers ) and it went sideways really quick when he went to L.A. with Luke [Walton]. "From the outside [Nurse and James] look like they're working together very well." James has indeed shown a positive relationship with Nurse, who is tapping into the 41-year-old's versatility and buy-in. For example, James has been used as the lead ball handler for sections of the games and, conversely, had shifted to defensive center with the Sixers managing injuries to their big men. Before the season, James praised Nurse specifically for the job he did with the Toronto Raptors , who won the franchise's first title in 2019 behind Nurse's guidance. "[LeBron] had a good relationship with JJ [Redick] from day one [with the Lakers] and they worked well together and that's a better way to live," a Western Conference assistant coach said. "If LeBron thinks you're smart and you put him in a position to be successful, he's going to respect you." MacMahon: Major offseason additions typically force teams into roster shuffling that create other issues -- consider the Miami Heat 's lack of depth after landing Giannis Antetokounmpo . But that hasn't been the case for Philadelphia, which gave up a starter in Paul George for an upgrade in Brown, then added James on a minimum deal. New Sixers president Mike Gansey also found value on the fringes, signing Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope in free agency this summer. "Their bench is [strong] outside of a backup big," an East scout said. "Simons might be the best bench scorer in the league. KCP is really good in the role that they have for him. You add one backup big and they have an A-plus rotation." The Sixers addressed that need by signing former Knick Ariel Hukporti , but the 7-footer is out for the season after tearing his Achilles in the preseason. Philadelphia's payroll is hard capped at the first apron ($1.8 million under the threshold), limiting any options to add frontcourt depth. Philadelphia would be an attractive destination in the buyout market after the Feb. 11 trade deadline, when the Sixers could squeeze a pro-rated minimum onto their books. But several executives around the league wondered how much the new anti-tanking lottery rules will weaken the buyout market. What are people saying about the Memphis Grizzlies hot start? MacMahon: The most pleasant surprise in the West so far? The 6-2 Grizzlies. "They've got a bunch of guys that are trying to prove themselves, but they play together," a West executive said. "They're very physical. Sometimes you get those teams where all the pieces fit together because everybody accepts their roles." Or, as a West scout put it: "Memphis is the Phoenix of last year," a team widely projected to finish in the lottery that will barge its way into the postseason. But there is one drastic difference between last season's Suns, who won 45 games and the 8-seed despite losing Kevin Durant , and these Grizzlies: It's easy to envision Memphis making significant strides over the next few seasons. Guard Ty Jerome 's sudden emergence as a scoring machine has commanded attention, but the Grizzlies' long-term foundation is the other four starters, all still on rookie contracts: Rookie of the Year contender Cameron Boozer , Cedric Coward , Zach Edey and Jaylen Wells . Memphis GM Zach Kleiman loaded up on draft capital during the deconstruction of the Grizzlies' previous era, as the team has nine tradable first-round picks, the most valuable being the Utah Jazz 's pick in 2027 and Suns' in 2031. The Grizzlies are also positioned to have significant salary cap space in the offseason. If the Grizzlies are aggressive before the 2027 trade deadline, anticipate a "pre-agency" move focused on the future. For example, if the Grizzlies have a potential restricted free agent they covet, Kleiman could trade for the player and secure his rights instead of trying to sign him to an offer sheet in the summer. No matter what, Kleiman is primed to add a significant player to an impressive young core. "For where they are in their arc, they're pretty freakin' good," a West coach said. Windhorst: Jerome's hot start seems to have transported us back two years. The Cavaliers were already expected to be a contender in 2024-25, but they surged out of the gates and Jerome's explosive scoring -- then in a lead bench role -- was a big reason they won 60 games. That came after he sat out almost all of the previous season because of injury. Well, Jerome sat out almost all of last season because of injury and kind of was forgotten again. Then, wham, he's healthy and sparking Memphis' fifth-ranked offense. "If you look at Ty's career, when he's been healthy he's always reliably been a real contributor. The teams who've had him have always loved him," a West executive said. "If he's healthy and playing and you put the ball in his hands, the guy is going to put up numbers. It's just been hard to get all three of those aligned year over year." There's no doubt the Grizzlies have benefitted from a favorable early schedule. Scouts expect them to find their level, but that might end up higher than most expected. "If they stay healthy they can be a .500 team and I think they'd absolutely have taken that at the start of the season," a West scout said. "Having some early success can be great for young guys. "You can see how sometimes young guys who are used to winning hang their heads when they get bashed early in the league. These guys, you can see their chests growing right now." What else are league personnel talking about this week? MacMahon: It's way too early for trade discussions to pick up steam, but multiple scouts and executives are keeping an eye on the LA Clippers as likely sellers. The Clippers, who are off to a league-worst-tying 1-7 start, have a handful of impact veterans on expiring contracts. Center Brook Lopez , guard Kris Dunn , forward Rui Hachimura (team option next season) and wings Max Strus and Derrick Jones Jr . all could fill roles for playoff teams. Windhorst: One of this early season's box score parlor games has been counting the shots Kings' rookie Darius Acuff Jr . takes (he's averaging a whopping 23.6) compared to All-Star teammate big man Domantas Sabonis (who is averaging 8.6, his lowest since his rookie year a decade ago). And Sabonis subtly criticized Acuff for it the first week of the season. But, subsequently, Sabonis has praised Acuff several times and has gone to lengths to support him. Sources in Sacramento insist that Sabonis has taken a liking to the 19-year-old, appreciates his immense scoring talent and enjoys the process of playing with Acuff as he learns the league. Does Sabonis like every shot Acuff takes? Unlikely. Would it benefit both the 30-year-old Sabonis and the Kings to find a trade partner? Likely. The same goes for Malik Monk and Zach LaVine . (They are the three oldest players on a rebuilding team that, to loosely paraphrase ESPN's Fran Fraschilla, is a year away from being a year away.) Be all of that as it may, we are told emphatically any perceived Sabonis-Acuff beef is a nonstory.

stories.title: Miami Heat unveil 'A Night in Vice City' jerseys ahead of GTA VI release
stories.summary: With Grand Theft Auto VI's long-awaited release date set for Nov. 19, the Heat are partnering with Rockstar Games to offer a topical lead-up event the night before.
stories.detailText: The Miami Heat have been carefully leaning into "Vice City" branding for years now , but 2026 will bring the team's most ambitious effort yet: Nov. 18 will be "A Night in Vice City" at the Kaseya Center. With Grand Theft Auto VI's long-awaited release date set for Nov. 19, the Heat are partnering with Rockstar Games to offer a topical lead-up event the night before. Miami is rolling out plenty of offerings for the night. The night will feature a special Vice-themed court and a reimagined edition of the team's popular alternate uniforms, as well as "special game night activities" and "unique game night activations." The jerseys, unveiled Friday, build on the team's past "Vice" alternates with nods to Grand Theft Auto VI and Travis Scott's Cactus Jack brand. The black Swingman jersey features pink and white accents, "Vice City" across the chest, Scott's signature flipped Nike Swoosh and a "VI" nod to the game. Six pink stars and Cactus Jack branding appear at the hem alongside a tag featuring Rockstar Games, the Heat and Cactus Jack. Both the on-court and Swingman versions will be available in limited quantities on Nov. 18. According to a news release, the special occasion will "transform the Kaseya Center into Vice City -- showcasing the Miami-inspired setting of Grand Theft Auto VI -- for a first-of-its-kind sports crossover experience." The Heat kicked off the promotion for the special event Thursday, lighting up "Welcome to Vice City" signage on the roof of the Kaseya Center. The team says it will share more information about "A Night in Vice City" in the coming weeks in coordination with Rockstar Games. The Heat's game that night against the Milwaukee Bucks will be broadcast on ESPN.

stories.title: Raptors look to claim first NBA Cup win
stories.summary: Raptors take on the Milwaukee Bucks in second NBA Cup game.
stories.detailText: The Toronto Raptors are looking to secure their first win in the Emirates NBA Cup this season as they take on the Milwaukee Bucks on Friday, November 6. The Raptors, who are currently 0-1 in the competition and are coming off of a 128-109 loss against the Denver Nuggets. Toronto has not been on great form, losing 3 of their last four and currently sit at 4-4. For the Bucks, their start to the season has been poor as they enter this contest with a record of 1-7 and are on a four-game losing streak. Both teams have work to do The Raptors have had many issues to start their season off, mainly surrounding slow starts to games, while not being able to finish games. Perimeter defence has also been a problem. There has also been massive vulnerability in the frontcourt and rebounding. While they’re strong on the offensive glass, their undersized or banged-up frontline has struggled to contain dominant opposing centres. With no true centre, the Raptors have struggled. They should be looking to make a trade for a well renowned centre to help them fix their issue there. Not having Kawhi Leonard has also seemed to affect the Raptors, as there is now more pressure on Scottie Barnes, Immanuel Quickley, and RJ Barrett to carry the load. For the Bucks, life without Giannis Antetokounmpo has been difficult. They are fielding a younger squad and are in a transitional period. The core now features players acquired in recent moves, such as Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., and Kel’el Ware from Miami, alongside veterans like Myles Turner and coach Doc Rivers (with assistant Darvin Ham) trying to install a new system. General execution and youth consistency have also been issues early in the year, the young and reshaped rotation (including rookie Brayden Burries and Ryan Rollins) has struggled with late-game execution, shooting efficiency, and closing out tight contests. To stay competitive, the Bucks must rely on Myles Turner and Kel’el Ware to control the glass and prevent Scottie Barnes and RJ Barrett from dominating the paint, while forcing Toronto into a perimeter shooting contest where they currently hit just 31.9 percent from deep. Ultimately, if Milwaukee’s Tyler Herro and AJ Green can capitalize on high-efficiency looks from three-point range to offset Toronto’s relentless downhill physicality, the Bucks can mask their defensive deficiencies and stall the Raptors’ high-volume possession game. This is a great time for the Bucks to win their second game of the year, as they face a Toronto side that has really struggled as of late. stories.title: Doc Rivers talks Giannis Antetokounmpo leaving Bucks, challenges of coaching superstar
stories.summary: "It's really a strange thing, and he really has one way: downhill, force, force. Every play."
stories.detailText: Giannis Antetokounmpo is one-of-one. He doesn't play in the style of other superstars, which makes coaching the NBA champion and two-time MVP a particular challenge. Doc Rivers, the former Bucks coach turned NBC Sports studio host for NBA broadcasts, pulled no punches when talking about how he found it difficult to coach Antetokounmpo in an appearance on the Bill Simmons podcast . Doc Rivers tells Bill Simmons it was so hard for him to coach Giannis Antetokounmpo during his tenure with the Milwaukee Bucks: “He’s not easy. He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He’s really a difficult guy. He has this great passing ability, but he doesn’t have a super-high… — Ahmed/The Ears/IG: BigBizTheGod (@big_business_) November 6, 2026 "I liked Giannis a lot. I liked him more as a dude. He's interesting. He's not easy. He's not easy because he plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy.... "He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have this super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing, and he really has one way: downhill, force, force. Every play, he wants to force it. I wish he learned how to execute better. He's one of those guys... that have never needed to execute because they can do it on their own. But that doesn't help the team. And I told Giannis this, the thing he needs to still learn is the value of execution. How important it is when you're in practice and shoot-arounds to lock in on execution. And now he has a coach [Erik Spoelstra] who is as good as there is in execution." Rivers came in at the end of Antetokounmpo's time in Milwaukee, taking over in the middle of the 2023-24 season, and the team never found a consistent identity under Rivers' leadership. Part of that was the personnel around Antetokounmpo at the time: Jrue Holiday was gone, Kris Middleton was battling injuries and not the same player as his peak, and Damian Lillard was supposed to be the "fix." Rivers also was there for Antetokounmpo's exit from Milwaukee, and he talked about that as well with Simmons. "Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. And he didn't want to be the bad guy. He wanted [GM Jon Horst and owner Wes Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played." That take is not controversial, that's how pretty much everyone saw Antetokounmpo's exit from Milwaukee. His comments on Antetokounmpo's play are going to draw pushback out of Miami.

stories.title: Giannis is playing defense like a toddler chasing a ball
stories.summary: Giannis’ defensive decline in one clip.
stories.detailText: It wasn’t long ago that Giannis Antetokounmpo was one of the NBA’s best defenders. He joined Michael Jordan and Hakeem Olajuwon as the third player ever to be named NBA MVP and Defensive Player of the Year in the same season during the 2019-2020 campaign, and he was consistently a major part of some great units in Milwaukee. Antetokounmpo was always at his best as a ‘roamer’ who could run around and make plays next to Brook Lopez’s reliable rim protection in drop coverage. Giannis is still roaming after his offseason trade to the Miami Heat , but he doesn’t look like the same defender he once was now that he’s on the brink of turning 32 years old. Antetokounmpo ranks outside of the top-100 in Dean Oliver’s Net-Points Defense stat , and he put some ugly flashes on tape Thursday night as the Golden State Warriors beat the Heat, 120-100. Antetokounmpo went viral on Thursday for an ugly clip of chasing the ball defensively with absolutely zero purpose. Giannis looked like a big golden retriever out there following the ball wherever it went without actually positioning himself to help make a defensive stop. Watch the clip here: Giannis is COMPLETELY lost on defense Bro just running around out there 😭 pic.twitter.com/LKgx8DNWzj — BrickCenter (@BrickCenter_) November 6, 2026 Giannis looks tired as hell in this clip, and that’s understandable. He’s the only real offensive creator on the Heat right now, and he’s not working with the type of spacing he enjoyed during his heyday with the Bucks. He’s putting up a 32.8% usage rate right now, and it’s probably too much to ask to carry that level of offensive burden while also being a great defender. Sharp observers have noticed Giannis’ defense starting to decline the last couple seasons. The Heat’s best pathway to success this season was being an elite defensive team, and I’m just not sure if they can get there. Miami fell to 3-6 after the loss to the Warriors, and they’re lucky to even be that good, because they needed an overtime buzzer-beater to defeat a terrible Los Angeles Clippers team in their previous game. There’s a lot of basketball left to be played, but the Giannis trade feels like a lose-lose for Milwaukee and Miami so far.
